edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SPORT + SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY
edition.deck: A besieged Yemeni city, new European talks on Ukraine and a closely watched UK-EU summit lead the morning’s coverage.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises overnight developments and consequential reporting. The Ukraine story distinguishes diplomatic claims from the continuing attacks; the Myanmar coverage focuses on the judgment’s possible legal significance rather than repeating yesterday’s verdict report.

content.headline: Residents describe hunger and danger as Houthis encircle Yemen’s Taiz
content.shortHeadline: Inside Taiz, cut off by Houthi forces
content.standfirst: Residents and a doctor in the government-controlled city tell the BBC that food, medicine and fuel are running short after Houthi forces encircled Taiz. The group denies the city is under siege.

image.caption: A view of Taiz, where residents report shortages and continuing Houthi attacks.

sources.originalTitle: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC

segments.body: Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, has been cut off since Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, the BBC reports. Seven residents described dwindling supplies, rising prices and dangerous journeys around the city. A teacher said she keeps her children indoors because shelling and sniper fire can make even a short trip unsafe.

segments.title: Shortages deepen the crisis
segments.body: A doctor told the BBC that his hospital was running low on supplies and might be able to continue for only two more weeks. Taiz’s governor said hospitals had lost much of their capacity and that shortages were also costing lives. The Houthis’ leader denies the city is besieged; residents, local officials, aid agencies and the UN dispute that account.

content.headline: Ukraine allies prepare for talks as Russia’s attacks continue
content.shortHeadline: Europe readies for Ukraine peace talks
content.standfirst: European leaders say they are ready to negotiate with Moscow, but Russia’s position and the terms of any talks remain uncertain. Kyiv was hit during the diplomatic meetings, with damage reported at several embassies.

image.caption: A police officer speaks with residents at a Kyiv apartment building damaged by a Russian drone strike.

sources.originalTitle: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
Ukraine war briefing: Trump ‘open’ to Kyiv getting Nato-like mutual defence guarantee, says Kushner
Merz tog et stykke af Berlinmuren med på pressemøde og sendte direkte budskab til Putin
EU vil indkalde russisk udsending efter skader på ambassader i Kyiv

segments.body: At a Berlin meeting of Ukraine’s allies, European leaders said they were prepared to join negotiations with Russia. US envoy Jared Kushner said Moscow was comfortable with Ukraine receiving an Article 5-style security guarantee; Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders remained cautious. Putin said Russia wanted to clarify Europe’s position before deciding how talks might proceed.

segments.title: Attacks underline the gap between talks and the war
segments.body: Russian strikes on Kyiv killed at least one person and damaged buildings, including the Dutch and Austrian embassies, according to reports from Berlin and Kyiv. The EU foreign-policy chief said the bloc would summon Russia’s envoy; the Netherlands and Sweden also said they would summon Russian representatives. Russia had not commented on the summons at the time of reporting.

perspectives.body: DR reports that the EU, the Netherlands and Sweden planned to summon Russian representatives after damage to diplomatic premises in Kyiv. The report says it was unclear whether a drone had targeted the area or was brought down there.

content.headline: Myanmar genocide judgment may shape future cases, legal experts say
content.shortHeadline: Myanmar ruling could influence future genocide cases
content.standfirst: The International Court of Justice’s ruling has clarified how genocidal intent can be established, according to legal experts. Its reasoning may be relevant to other cases, but does not determine their outcomes.

image.caption: Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh watch the International Court of Justice deliver its ruling.

sources.originalTitle: Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
Professor i folkeret: Myanmars dom for folkedrab kan få betydning for Israel

segments.body: The ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, in a ruling that could influence how future cases are argued. BBC international editor Jeremy Bowen reports that the judges considered the totality of the evidence in assessing intent, rather than requiring genocide to be the only possible purpose behind the actions.

perspectives.body: Danish legal expert Frederik Harhoff says the ruling reaffirms the definition of genocide and may be relevant to South Africa’s case against Israel. He stresses that the court cannot impose prison sentences on individuals or enforce its own decisions.

segments.title: A possible legal influence, not a forecast
segments.body: The reasoning may matter in South Africa’s case alleging genocide in Gaza, but it does not decide that case. Israel strongly rejects the allegation. The court has ordered Myanmar to pay reparations to Rohingya victims, but it has no enforcement mechanism of its own and implementation will depend on political action.

content.headline: Pancreatic cancer pill shows promise in early trial, researchers say
content.shortHeadline: Early trial finds promise in pancreatic cancer pill
content.standfirst: With chemotherapy, daraxonrasib made tumours undetectable on scans in some participants and stopped them growing in almost all of a small trial group. Researchers stress that longer studies are needed.

sources.originalTitle: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish

segments.body: In an early trial involving 61 people with advanced pancreatic cancer, tumours stopped growing in almost all participants who received daraxonrasib alongside chemotherapy. Cancer was undetectable on scans in one in 12. The results are being presented to doctors, and Cancer Research UK called them a major advance for a disease that is difficult to treat.

segments.title: What remains unknown
segments.body: The study followed patients for an average of a year and a half. Doctors say it is too soon to know how long the cancer may stay controlled, whether the treatment will extend survival, or whether tumours that cannot be seen on scans have been eliminated. The findings should not be taken as evidence of a cure.

content.headline: Canada courts AI data centres as US communities push back
content.shortHeadline: Canada bets on AI data centres amid US backlash
content.standfirst: Canadian provinces are pitching land, energy and fast approvals to attract data-centre investment, while projects face opposition over power, water and environmental risks. A major Alberta proposal is also being challenged in court.

image.caption: Kevin O’Leary is behind a proposed AI data-centre project in Alberta.

sources.originalTitle: Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back

segments.body: As opposition to data-centre projects grows in the US, Canadian leaders are seeking to attract investment. Alberta has backed a proposed 7,000-acre facility that would use natural gas to generate its own power. The project still needs permits, and the provincial government exempted it from an environmental impact assessment.

segments.title: Local consent remains a question
segments.body: The proposed Alberta site would use an estimated six million cubic metres of water each year, prompting concern from some residents. Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation has sued over the assessment exemption. While governments point to jobs and investment, researchers and residents warn that public opposition could grow if development is not handled carefully.

content.headline: California investigates Nvidia over allegations involving China
content.shortHeadline: California opens Nvidia probe over China allegations
content.standfirst: California’s attorney general is investigating whether Nvidia or its former chief executive’s actions led to advanced chips or confidential information reaching China. The company had not commented on the investigation.

sources.originalTitle: California targets Nvidia in China AI chip probe

segments.body: California Attorney General Rob Bonta said his office had served Nvidia with an investigative subpoena. The inquiry will examine whether the company or former chief executive Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, and whether any conduct could have misled investors or the public. Nvidia had not responded to the BBC’s request for comment.

The investigation follows reports about Huang’s relationship with an executive at data-centre company Megaspeed and congressional calls to examine whether Nvidia chips were diverted to China. Megaspeed has said claims about its business and supply chain are not supported by verifiable evidence. The reported allegations have not been established by the probe.

content.headline: US Army delays Iowa blast of unstable explosives after safety concerns
content.shortHeadline: Iowa explosives blast delayed amid toxic-plume fears
content.standfirst: The Army has postponed detonating five tonnes of degrading lead azide until Monday, after residents and environmental groups raised concerns about toxic dust. The Army says the material is too unstable to move safely.

image.caption: The Army says detonating the unstable material in place is the safest disposal option.

sources.originalTitle: US army warns detonation of unstable explosives will create toxic plume

segments.body: The US Army plans to detonate the material at its ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, after a routine check found that some water used to stabilise the lead azide had evaporated. The Army says it is safer to destroy the material in place than to move it. The operation, first scheduled for Friday, was delayed until Monday.

segments.title: Residents and environmental groups object
segments.body: The Army warns that the explosions could send lead-containing dust over parts of Iowa and neighbouring Illinois, and has asked residents to leave or remain indoors during the operation. Two environmental groups have sued to stop it, arguing that safer alternatives were not adequately considered. The Army says barriers and water-soaked soil will be used to reduce airborne lead.

content.headline: UK and EU near youth mobility deal ahead of Brussels summit
content.shortHeadline: UK and EU near deal on youth mobility
content.standfirst: Negotiators have provisionally agreed a 100,000-person annual cap on a youth scheme, while a compromise on student fees is also reported. Leaders are due to discuss the wider reset package at Friday’s summit.

image.caption: Andy Burnham and European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen at the UN General Assembly.

sources.originalTitle: UK and EU to agree youth mobility scheme, BBC understands
UK and EU close to post-Brexit deal as they agree 100,000 youth mobility cap
What is at stake at the EU-UK summit in Brussels?

segments.body: The UK and EU are close to agreeing a youth mobility scheme that would let up to 100,000 young people from each side travel, work and study across the Channel each year, the BBC reports. The proposed age range is 18 to 31. The agreement is expected to be considered at Friday’s summit in Brussels.

segments.title: Other parts of the reset remain in play
segments.body: The Guardian reports that the EU dropped its demand for EU students to pay domestic tuition fees, with further negotiations expected on a reduced-fee arrangement. The sides are also seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon pricing. The details and final outcome of the summit were still pending at the time of reporting.

content.headline: UK and EU plan talks on returning rejected asylum seekers to third countries
content.shortHeadline: UK and EU to discuss third-country asylum returns
content.standfirst: A draft summit statement would open a formal dialogue on returns to third countries. The UK says it is exploring options, but the proposed talks do not amount to an agreed returns scheme.

sources.originalTitle: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries
UK open to joining future European Rwanda migrant return scheme

segments.body: A draft statement for Friday’s UK-EU summit proposes a structured dialogue on migration, including returns to third countries for people whose asylum claims have been rejected. The proposal would be the first formal UK-EU discussion of this kind. It was not yet an agreed policy or an operating scheme.

segments.title: The model remains uncertain
segments.body: The UK government says it supports exploring returns hubs, and a minister told the i Paper that Britain was watching a plan involving Rwanda with close interest. That European plan concerns people who have exhausted legal routes and differs from the scrapped UK scheme, which would have sent people to have their asylum claims processed in Rwanda. Refugee advocates warn that third-country removals could be costly and distressing.

perspectives.body: The i Paper reports that the proposed European arrangement would apply after migrants had exhausted legal avenues, unlike the former UK plan to send people to Rwanda for their claims to be processed.

content.headline: Lawyer seeks urgent review of Lucy Letby convictions after witness revelations
content.shortHeadline: Letby lawyer seeks urgent review after witness revelations
content.standfirst: A key prosecution expert was barred by his hospital from treating patients over safety concerns during Letby’s trial, the Guardian reports. Her lawyer says the information should prompt an urgent review; no court has overturned her convictions.

sources.originalTitle: Lawyer calls for urgent review of Letby convictions after expert witness revelations

segments.body: Lucy Letby’s lawyer is asking the Criminal Cases Review Commission to refer her convictions back to the Court of Appeal. The request follows reporting that Prof Peter Hindmarsh, whose evidence was important to the prosecution’s insulin-poisoning case, had been barred from clinical practice by his hospital while the trial was underway.

segments.title: Questions about disclosure
segments.body: The jury was not told of the hospital restriction or a tribunal order requiring Hindmarsh to be supervised in clinical work. The CPS says it was not informed of those developments. Letby’s lawyer argues the information could have affected the defence; legal experts quoted by the Guardian say non-disclosure about an expert may be relevant to an appeal, depending on the facts. Letby remains convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others.

content.headline: Bradford councillor stabbed while canvassing; man arrested
content.shortHeadline: Bradford councillor stabbed; man arrested
content.standfirst: Independent councillor Ibrar Ali is in hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries after an attack while canvassing. Police say there is no indication yet that it was politically motivated.

image.caption: Bradford councillor Ibrar Ali.

sources.originalTitle: Man arrested after ‘horrific’ knife attack on Bradford councillor

segments.body: A 32-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after councillor Ibrar Ali was stabbed in Bradford on Thursday. Ali was taken to hospital with injuries described by police as serious but not life-threatening. Police said the investigation was at an early stage and there was nothing to suggest a political motive.

content.headline: NHS hospitals to offer Alzheimer’s blood tests before trials conclude
content.shortHeadline: Hospitals to expand access to Alzheimer’s blood tests
content.standfirst: Some NHS hospitals plan to introduce blood tests for Alzheimer’s from early next year, potentially speeding diagnosis. Availability is likely to vary, and large trials are still under way.

image.caption: A blood test could help shorten the time needed to investigate memory problems.

sources.originalTitle: The simple test that will diagnose Alzheimer’s within days – available next year

segments.body: A blood test measuring a form of tau protein could help doctors assess whether memory problems are caused by Alzheimer’s. Some hospitals are preparing to offer the test through memory clinics or neurology departments, with Manchester Brain Health Centre saying it expects to begin in the coming weeks. Diagnosis can currently take months or longer.

segments.title: Access and evidence remain limited
segments.body: Two large trials assessing how the tests fit into NHS care are due to finish in 2029, and there is no central register of which hospitals currently offer them. People outside participating hospitals may have to pay privately. Doctors warn that tests taken outside a clinical assessment could produce false positives; a result needs to be interpreted alongside a patient’s symptoms and examination.

content.headline: UK-EU summit draft includes talks on third-country asylum returns
content.shortHeadline: UK and EU draft plans migration dialogue
content.standfirst: The proposed dialogue would cover returns to third countries, a potentially significant addition to the reset agenda. It remains a draft and does not establish where or how anyone would be removed.

sources.originalTitle: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries

segments.body: A draft joint statement for the UK-EU summit would establish a structured dialogue on migration, including returns to third countries. The discussions would sit alongside cooperation on border management and action against smuggling networks. The draft was expected to be considered by leaders on Friday.

content.headline: NAO warns next BBC cuts may be more noticeable to audiences
content.shortHeadline: Next BBC cuts may be more visible to audiences
content.standfirst: A National Audit Office report says the BBC will face harder choices as it works towards a £500m savings target. It also says the corporation has not properly tracked the cumulative effect of cuts on audiences and services.

sources.originalTitle: Next round of BBC cuts will be more noticeable to audiences, report warns

segments.body: The National Audit Office says the BBC’s next round of cost reductions is likely to be harder to deliver and more noticeable to audiences. The corporation has already announced job, programme and service cuts but still has savings to make. The NAO says the workforce is expected to shrink by 11% over three years.

The report says licence-fee income has fallen in real terms over the past decade and weekly use of BBC services has declined. It also criticises the BBC for not properly monitoring the accumulated effect of earlier savings on audiences, service quality and its ability to deliver. The corporation says the savings programme is on track and that it accepts the NAO’s recommendations.

content.headline: Rigshospitalet says capacity limits led it to reject 12 donor livers
content.shortHeadline: Rigshospitalet rejected 12 donor livers over capacity
content.standfirst: Five of the livers might have been suitable for children, the hospital’s latest report says. It says the figures do not mean 12 patients could have received transplants, and that urgent cases were checked for a match.

image.caption: Rigshospitalet in Copenhagen.

sources.originalTitle: Rigshospitalet opjusterer: Har afvist 12 donorlevere på grund af manglende kapacitet

segments.body: Rigshospitalet rejected 12 donor livers between October 2025 and September 2026 because of capacity constraints, according to a new report from the Capital Region. Five could potentially have been used for a child. The figure is higher than the 10 previously reported.

segments.title: Staffing pressures extend to other operations
segments.body: The hospital says the rejected offers do not mean 12 Danish patients could have received transplants, since compatibility was not established in each case. It says urgent cases were always checked for a match and that no patient with an acute, life-threatening need was affected. The report also describes shortages of specialist surgeons for liver transplants and pancreatic cancer operations.

content.headline: Police suspect man killed partner and daughter before taking his own life
content.shortHeadline: Police suspect man killed partner and daughter in Give
content.standfirst: Initial findings suggest a 62-year-old man killed his partner and their 10-year-old daughter before taking his own life, police say. The circumstances remain under investigation.

sources.originalTitle: Politi: Mand dræbte kæreste og datter i Give

segments.body: Police say preliminary findings suggest a 62-year-old man killed his 48-year-old partner and their 10-year-old daughter in Give before taking his own life. The three were found dead at their home on Wednesday. Police have not said how or when they believe the deaths occurred and say the investigation is continuing.

content.headline: Man dies after explosion and fire in container in Hornslet
content.shortHeadline: Man dies after container explosion in Hornslet
content.standfirst: A 69-year-old man died after an explosion involving a container with gas cylinders in an industrial area. Police say initial investigations point to an accident.

sources.originalTitle: 69-årig mand død efter eksplosion i container i Hornslet

segments.body: A 69-year-old man was found near a container after an explosion and fire at an industrial area in Hornslet on Thursday. Fire officials said the container held pressurised cylinders and the blast damaged a nearby warehouse. Police said initial investigations indicated that the incident was an accident.

content.headline: Police warn residents to close windows during warehouse fire in Mørke
content.shortHeadline: Asbestos warning during warehouse fire in Mørke
content.standfirst: The old warehouse was almost burned down, and police say its roof contains asbestos. There are no reports of injuries; people nearby have been told to keep windows and doors closed.

sources.originalTitle: Politi til stede ved brand i lagerbygning i Mørke - luk vinduer og døre

segments.body: Police and firefighters were responding to a fire at an old warehouse on Industrivej in Mørke, Djursland, early Friday. The building was almost burned down, and crews were working to prevent the fire spreading to nearby buildings. Police said there were no reports of injuries and warned people in the area to keep doors and windows closed because the roof contains asbestos.

content.headline: Repeated bicycle-shop burglaries cost North Jutland businesses millions
content.shortHeadline: Bicycle thefts cost North Jutland shops millions
content.standfirst: One shop in Støvring says thieves have taken bicycles worth more than DKK 3m in three break-ins since March. Another shop in Aars was targeted a day later, and police are investigating both cases.

image.caption: Støvring bicycle-shop owner Simon Lassen describes the repeated break-ins.

sources.originalTitle: Siden foråret har Simon mistet cykler for flere millioner kroner

segments.body: A bicycle shop in Støvring says it lost bicycles worth about DKK 750,000 in a break-in this week, despite spending more than DKK 300,000 on extra security after earlier thefts. It estimates losses across three break-ins since March at more than DKK 3m.

A shop in Aars was burgled about a day later, with its owner saying thieves selected high-value bicycles. He had not yet established the total loss. North Jutland Police said they were investigating both cases and had received information from residents and local businesses.

content.headline: England fined after away fans chant anti-Catholic abuse in Spain
content.shortHeadline: England fined over anti-Catholic chants in Spain
content.standfirst: Uefa fined the Football Association £12,572 and imposed a suspended one-match ban on England away supporters after chants deemed anti-Catholic and anti-Irish during the 3-2 Nations League win in Spain.

sources.originalTitle: England fined for fans' anti-Catholic chants in Spain

segments.body: Uefa fined the Football Association £12,572 (15,000 euros) and suspended England away supporters from one match. BBC Sport understands the charge of “racist and/or discriminatory behaviour” relates to chants deemed anti-Catholic and anti-Irish during England’s 3-2 win in Madrid.
The away-fan ban will be enforced if there is a further offence within two years. England’s victory also ended Spain’s 43-match unbeaten run and put England top of their Nations League group.

content.headline: Lyon expose Arsenal's gap to Europe's Women's Champions League elite
content.shortHeadline: Lyon expose Arsenal's European gap
content.standfirst: Arsenal were outplayed in a 2-0 home defeat by Lyon, their second demanding test against a European heavyweight in a week. The result leaves them needing to improve both their form and their chances of progressing.

image.caption: Arsenal goalkeeper Misa Rodríguez made six saves in the defeat by Lyon.

sources.originalTitle: Arsenal 'have ingredients' but Europe's elite on another level

segments.body: Jule Brand put Lyon ahead midway through the first half and Melchie Dumornay sealed the 2-0 win in the 57th minute. Lyon had 23 shots to Arsenal’s seven and created six big chances; Arsenal goalkeeper Misa Rodríguez made six saves.

segments.title: The challenge ahead
segments.body: Arsenal had drawn 1-1 away to Barcelona the previous week, but the defeat by Lyon followed a fifth successive Women’s Super League draw at home. Arsenal have not yet qualified for the Champions League knockout stages and are 12 points off the WSL title pace.

content.headline: Shevchenko rejects Mudryk's claim that Ukraine FA caused failed drugs test
content.shortHeadline: Shevchenko rebuts Mudryk over failed drugs test
content.standfirst: Mykhailo Mudryk blames Ukraine’s football association for the meldonium finding that led to his 20-month suspension. Andriy Shevchenko says the accusation is baseless and calls on the winger to provide evidence or apologise.

image.caption: Mykhailo Mudryk, who has 28 caps for Ukraine.

sources.originalTitle: Shevchenko accuses Mudryk camp of 'baseless slander'

segments.body: Mudryk, who returned to football in July after a suspension running from November 2024, says the Ukrainian Association of Football was responsible for his failed test and that the substance entered his system on international duty. He also criticised the association’s handling of the case and said Shevchenko offered little support.

segments.title: The association's response
segments.body: Shevchenko, now UAF president, says Mudryk’s representatives repeatedly asked the association to find an employee to falsely accept responsibility for the meldonium finding, and that it refused. He says investigations and audits did not establish when or where the substance entered Mudryk’s system, and challenged him to provide evidence. BBC Sport has contacted Mudryk’s representatives for comment.

content.headline: England recall Furbank, Atkinson and Chessum for New Zealand test
content.shortHeadline: England bring back three starters for All Blacks test
content.standfirst: George Furbank, Seb Atkinson and Ollie Chessum return to England’s starting side for Saturday’s Nations Championship meeting with New Zealand. Will Joseph keeps his place after scoring five tries against Japan.

image.caption: George Furbank returns to England's starting side at full-back.

sources.originalTitle: Furbank leads returning England trio for All Blacks visit
'Clearer' approach has lifted England mood - Itoje

segments.body: Furbank returns at full-back, Atkinson at centre and Chessum in the back row after all three missed last weekend’s win over Japan with knocks. Fin Smith is back at fly-half, while Joseph starts again after crossing five times in the 45-12 victory.

segments.title: A test of England's progress
segments.body: England have won their past four matches, including a 45-12 victory over Australia, after a run of five successive defeats. Captain Maro Itoje says the team’s purpose and understanding have become clearer; coach Steve Borthwick has also credited senior players’ work on discipline. New Zealand arrive after losing to Wales for the first time in 73 years.

perspectives.body: Itoje describes England as more cohesive, with a clearer understanding of their game plan. Borthwick says senior players led discussions on discipline, following 14 yellow cards and a red in England’s first eight Tests of 2026; the team has had no cards across its two November Tests so far.

content.headline: Zverev tops ATP Finals group but raises ankle concern; Shelton also advances
content.shortHeadline: Zverev wins group as Shelton reaches ATP Finals semis
content.standfirst: Alexander Zverev beat Arthur Fils in straight sets to finish top of his ATP Finals group, but said his troublesome right ankle was painful. Ben Shelton also secured a semi-final place after beating Rafael Jodar.

image.caption: Alexander Zverev, who won his ATP Finals group despite an ankle problem.

sources.originalTitle: Unbeaten Zverev hopes to be 'pain-free' after overcoming Fils at ATP Finals

segments.body: Zverev won 6-4 7-6 (8-6), finishing top of the John McEnroe Group and sending Shelton through. He said pain in the right ankle—where he tore ligaments in 2022—affected his serve, and that he would do everything he could to be pain-free for Saturday’s semi-final.

Shelton had beaten Jodar 7-6 (10-8) 7-5 earlier, a result that left his qualification dependent on Zverev beating Fils. Zverev has yet to lose a set in Turin, but his semi-final availability remains uncertain given the ankle problem he described.

content.headline: Charley Hull one shot off lead after opening round at LPGA finale
content.shortHeadline: Hull one off lead at LPGA season finale
content.standfirst: Charley Hull opened the CME Group Tour Championship with a six-under-par 66, one shot behind three co-leaders. Fellow English golfer Lottie Woad is two shots off the pace after a five-under round.

image.caption: Charley Hull, who won this tournament in 2016.

sources.originalTitle: England's Hull one stroke off lead at lucrative LPGA finale

segments.body: Hull made 66 at Tiburon Golf Club in Naples, Florida, putting her among nine players one shot behind Karis Davidson, Kim A-lim and Jeeno Thitikul, who share the first-round lead at seven under. Woad signed for a five-under 67.

content.headline: World marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir given three-year doping ban
content.shortHeadline: Jepchirchir banned for three years over doping violation
content.standfirst: The Athletics Integrity Unit says a sample collected before Peres Jepchirchir’s Sydney Marathon win tested positive for EPO. The Kenyan denies using the substance but accepted disqualification of results from 17 July 2026.

image.caption: Peres Jepchirchir won the 2026 Sydney Marathon before the doping violation came to light.

sources.originalTitle: World marathon champion Jepchirchir gets three-year doping ban

segments.body: Jepchirchir, the reigning world marathon champion and 2021 Olympic gold medallist, has been banned for three years. The out-of-competition sample was collected in Kenya before her 30 August Sydney Marathon win and returned an adverse finding on 17 September. She denied using EPO but signed an admission of violations form and accepted disqualification of all results since 17 July 2026.

segments.title: Wider scrutiny
segments.body: The ban adds to scrutiny of Kenya’s anti-doping efforts ahead of its hosting of the 2029 World Athletics Championships. More than 140 Kenyan athletes have been suspended by the AIU since 2017. The AIU has previously said it found no evidence of systemic violations, while recurring cases continue to raise questions about prevention and enforcement.

content.headline: LIV Golf paid players millions while UK suppliers were owed overdue bills
content.shortHeadline: LIV paid golfers millions as UK suppliers went unpaid
content.standfirst: BBC Sport has seen overdue invoices from five UK businesses as LIV Golf made millions in player payments before filing for bankruptcy. Small suppliers say the unpaid debts have put their businesses under severe strain.

sources.originalTitle: UK firms owed thousands as Saudi-backed LIV paid golfers millions

segments.body: Court filings show LIV made 59 payments to golfers totalling $16.6m on 31 July, while UK suppliers had overdue bills. A further $34.2m went to players between 17 August and 3 September; Jon Rahm received $6.4m five days before the league filed for bankruptcy protection on 8 September.

segments.title: Suppliers face uncertain recovery
segments.body: Five small UK businesses provided BBC Sport with invoices totalling hundreds of thousands of pounds. Global Infusion Group is owed £321,671 and cleaning firm BD365 Clean £75,225. LIV did not respond to a request for comment. The Saudi owners have earmarked $2m for unsecured creditors so far, and a January hearing is due to consider the wind-down plan; how much suppliers will recover remains unknown.

content.headline: Why Gen Z are falling for Jeff Buckley’s songs of yearning
content.shortHeadline: Gen Z find their yearning anthem in Jeff Buckley
content.standfirst: Streams, TikTok searches and a flourishing market for memorabilia point to a revival of Buckley’s music among young listeners. Fans describe its unguarded emotion as a contrast to online life and the difficulty of finding connection.

image.caption: Sydney Tripoli with memorabilia from her Jeff Buckley collection.

sources.originalTitle: Jeff Buckley was a 90s indie darling. Now gen Z think he’s the ‘yearner final boss’

segments.body: Nearly three decades after Jeff Buckley’s death at 30, young listeners are finding their way to his sole lifetime album, Grace. Fans interviewed for this report describe its mix of romance and despair as speaking to a generation drawn to the feeling of longing, even when real-world connection can seem hard to reach.

segments.title: A revival across platforms
segments.body: The report points to rising streams since 2022, more than 500,000 TikToks using “Lover, You Should Have Come Over” this year, and a recent increase in searches for Buckley. A documentary has also brought former partner Rebecca Moore’s account into wider view, presenting a more human portrait than the familiar mythology around the singer.

content.headline: Life Without Buildings return after a quarter-century away
content.shortHeadline: Life Without Buildings return after 25 years
content.standfirst: The Glasgow group’s unconventional music found a new audience through Frank Ocean and TikTok. Their reunion has brought back both the excitement of playing together and the fear of disturbing a once-cherished moment.

image.caption: Life Without Buildings around the release of their debut album.

sources.originalTitle: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?

segments.body: Life Without Buildings played together for only three years before splitting in 2002. Their album Any Other City was met with a hostile review at the time, but the band’s singular songs and Sue Tompkins’s rhythmic, carefully written vocals later found new listeners after Frank Ocean played “The Leanover” and Beabadoobee’s TikTok helped it travel further.

segments.title: Protecting the joy
segments.body: The four members had decided not to reunite, worried that returning might spoil what they remembered as a beautiful, self-contained chapter. A secret Glasgow show for charity shifted that feeling: the musicians found their old interlocking sound still alive, and Tompkins described feeling both afraid and energised by the performance.

content.headline: Kate Nash turns industry frustration into a new Irish-rooted album
content.shortHeadline: Kate Nash brings her Irish roots to a new album
content.standfirst: The singer’s forthcoming Cailín draws on Irish instruments and family history, while her campaigning continues to focus on the economics that make touring difficult for working musicians.

image.caption: Kate Nash.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business

segments.body: Kate Nash says she still needs unconventional ways to fund touring, despite earning from her catalogue. Her “Butts for Tour Buses” campaign used an OnlyFans account to help pay for a tour, and she argues that the industry’s economics threaten the mid-sized and smaller gigs that sustain musical culture.

segments.title: Making Cailín
segments.body: Her new album, recorded in Spiddal on Ireland’s west coast, explores her Irish heritage through uilleann pipes, flutes and tin whistle alongside punk and hip-hop. Nash says recording it helped her learn more about her family history, including her grandfather’s attempted journey to fight Franco’s forces in Spain.

content.headline: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul find grief beneath the jokes
content.shortHeadline: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul turn inward
content.standfirst: The Belgian duo’s next album keeps their playful art-pop but moves towards grief, family and parenthood. Their tour of Ghent and conversation about the record reveal the personal history behind its stranger images.

image.caption: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul in Ghent.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Would you breastfeed your own father?’ The goofy, spiky world of art-pop duo Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul

segments.body: After a debut that used wit and dance-pop to examine race, colonialism and online life, Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul say their next album, Mainland Madinina, is more introspective. They began writing in Martinique, where Adigéry’s family roots helped shape a record about growing older, raising children and processing loss.

segments.title: A new emotional register
segments.body: Adigéry’s father died between the two albums, and the new songs include “I’m Lost”, about finally throwing away flowers from his funeral. The duo say humour remains, but grief has changed the work: writing and performing the songs offered Adigéry a way to consider what family trauma is passed on and what might be left behind.

content.headline: Radie Peat’s solo debut lets her voice reshape traditional folk
content.shortHeadline: Radie Peat reshapes folk on her solo debut
content.standfirst: The Lankum singer’s first solo album moves through Irish, British and American song traditions, with inventive arrangements that keep her commanding voice at the centre.

sources.originalTitle: No Human Tongue Can Tell

segments.body: Radie Peat opens No Human Tongue Can Tell with a stark rendition of the traditional “Hares on the Mountain”. From there, the Lankum and ØXN singer makes her voice the record’s anchor, layering it across songs whose arrangements move between keyboards, concertina and more unexpected textures.

segments.title: Old songs, altered
segments.body: The album draws on songs from Irish, British and American traditions, often centring women with complicated lives. Its standout transformation, the review argues, is “The Moon and Stars”: a fiddle tune recast as a dense, trip-hop-leaning piece that builds to a crashing finish without losing the force of Peat’s singing.

content.headline: Thoom fuses hyperpop and Arabic sounds into an emotionally vivid debut
content.shortHeadline: Thoom makes hyperpop personal on a vivid debut
content.standfirst: On Everyday, Everything Is at Stake, the Beirut-born, Los Angeles-based artist joins hyperpop production with Arabic instrumentation and a forceful vocal performance, turning emotional conflict into music of scale.

sources.originalTitle: Everyday, Everything Is at Stake

segments.body: Zeynab Marwan, who records as Thoom, brings contrasting energies together on her debut mixtape: club music’s abrasive force, pop drama and Arabic instrumentation. Her voice is central, shifting from syrupy melody to a menacing edge as the production moves through oud, mizmar, drum machines and restless synths.

segments.title: Belonging and uncertainty
segments.body: The closing “I’m Going Back to Lebanon” holds two unresolved desires at once: to leave a lover and to return home. Its questions about whether the artist can go back connect the mixtape’s emotional intensity to Lebanon’s ongoing crisis, making the song, in the review’s view, its clearest expression of what the title puts at stake.

content.headline: Lorenzo Senni brings punk screams into his restless electronic world
content.shortHeadline: Lorenzo Senni collides punk with electronic music
content.standfirst: All Ages draws on the Milan producer’s teenage straight-edge punk years and his fascination with rave. Its collision of beatless synths and raw voices is often thrilling, even when the experiment falters.

image.caption: Lorenzo Senni.

sources.originalTitle: Trance, prog synths, guttural screaming: Lorenzo Senni’s All Ages is the year’s wildest electronic album

segments.body: Lorenzo Senni has built a career at a distance from the dancefloor, dissecting trance rather than simply making club music. On All Ages, he turns towards his own past as a straight-edge punk fan and sets guttural hardcore vocals against his familiar, beatless flurries of synths.

segments.title: When the voices take hold
segments.body: Samples from Refused’s Dennis Lyxzén and the late Tim Taylor, among others, give tracks such as “Self eXamined Endurance” a propulsive quality in place of a conventional beat. The review finds the mix of punk and electronics most persuasive there, while some choices, including the piano-and-strings “Purely Coincidental”, feel less connected to the album’s central idea.

content.headline: U2’s Carnaval De Luz finds renewed purpose in familiar sounds
content.shortHeadline: U2 reconnect with their strengths on Carnaval De Luz
content.standfirst: The band’s first new album since 2017 trades some of their more portentous habits for open-hearted songs. This review hears a strong return, while questioning whether it can restore their wider cultural standing.

sources.originalTitle: U2 lost the plot decades ago – their new album finally fixes that

segments.body: Carnaval De Luz revisits familiar U2 ingredients: soaring choruses, The Edge’s guitar and songs about community and hope. The review argues that a lighter touch gives the band’s first album since 2017 a renewed energy and makes it their strongest record in years.

segments.title: A comeback in a changed landscape
segments.body: The album’s self-references can feel deliberate, and not every song works; “The Mirror Maker (Rosalía)” is singled out as an awkward tribute. The review also cautions that a good record may not restore U2’s former dominance in a splintered music culture where rock no longer commands the same attention.

content.headline: You Can See Everything turns Elizabeth Holmes into a shifting target
content.shortHeadline: Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes film keeps shifting
content.standfirst: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s film begins with access to Holmes before prison, then takes a startling turn. Its provocative use of reenactment leaves the viewer weighing performance against truth.

image.caption: Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.

sources.originalTitle: You Can See Everything review – unblinking, unhinged and unmissable

segments.body: Nathan Fielder spends time with Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before she went to prison, as she continues to insist that Theranos’s technology works. The review describes their conversations as a tense contest of polite faces, with Holmes’s certainty and evasions leaving Fielder—and the viewer—unsure how much she believes her own claims.

segments.title: Reenactment as a provocation
segments.body: After Holmes is sent to prison, Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim bring in Amanda Seyfried, who played Holmes in The Dropout, to recreate conversations they could not film. The device shifts the film’s focus from what Holmes may be concealing to the roles people perform, while leaving open how much of the story’s mystery has been shaped by editing.

content.headline: Josephine confronts sexual violence through a child’s perspective
content.shortHeadline: Josephine explores a child’s trauma after witnessing rape
content.standfirst: Beth de Araújo’s film follows an eight-year-old who witnesses a rape and struggles to understand what she saw. Its approach is grounded in the director’s experience, though one review finds some of its choices contrived.

image.caption: Channing Tatum and Mason Reeves in Josephine.

sources.originalTitle: 'The subject is still taboo': Shocking new film Josephine confronts sexual violence through a child's eyes
Josephine review – Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan ballast knotty drama about a child witness to a rape

segments.body: In Josephine, an eight-year-old girl witnesses a rape in a San Francisco park. Director Beth de Araújo says the story draws on her own childhood experience and asks viewers to imagine a child learning what sexual violence is through a moment she cannot yet process. The film also follows the effects on Josephine’s parents, played by Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan.

segments.title: A difficult question of representation
segments.body: De Araújo and film scholar Tanya Horeck discuss the ethics of showing sexual violence on screen, including what a rape scene is doing and whose perspective it serves. The Guardian review praises young lead Mason Reeves but finds the film’s recurring image of the attacker and parts of its courtroom plot contrived, underlining that the film’s bold subject does not remove questions about execution.

perspectives.body: The Guardian review calls Reeves outstanding but argues that the film’s repeated use of the attacker as a silent presence becomes contrived, and that its courtroom ending leaves an important real-world question unresolved.

content.headline: Anthony Boyle moves between a struggling courier and a crypto founder
content.shortHeadline: Anthony Boyle on playing a courier and Sam Bankman-Fried
content.standfirst: The Belfast-born actor discusses I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, about precarious work, and his role as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists. He says the characters have left him thinking about the distance between money and power.

image.caption: Anthony Boyle.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Sam-Bankman Fried messaged me from prison’: rising star Anthony Boyle on playing the disgraced tech bro – and a zero-hours bike courier

segments.body: Anthony Boyle plays Patrick, a politically outspoken bike courier supporting a young family on zero-hours work, in I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning. Boyle says the character’s struggle to get by should remind audiences that people live on precarious wages, adding that he hopes viewers might think about tipping a delivery worker.

segments.title: A very different kind of role
segments.body: Boyle also plays FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists. He says he exchanged more than 100 questions with Bankman-Fried through a prison messaging service, though he promised not to reveal what they discussed. Boyle draws a contrast between Patrick’s financial insecurity and the wealth associated with Bankman-Fried, saying his own focus is on doing good work rather than money.

content.headline: Wicker’s strange romance turns domestic expectations upside down
content.shortHeadline: Wicker makes a strange, funny case for equal partnership
content.standfirst: A woman commissions a husband made of willow in a bawdy, deliberately odd fairy tale. The film’s creators and commentators connect its appeal to domestic labour and desire; one critic finds its gender politics troubling but funny.

image.caption: Olivia Colman as the Fisherwoman in Wicker.

sources.originalTitle: A husband made from a basket? Why women are going wild for freaky film romance Wicker
Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it

segments.body: In Wicker, Olivia Colman plays an ostracised fisherwoman who commissions a basketmaker to make her a husband, played by Alexander Skarsgård. The filmmakers say the premise grew into a story about domestic labour, dating and the pressures women face in relationships, even as its fairy-tale village and sex comedy keep the tone deliberately strange.

segments.title: Fantasy, agency and laughter
segments.body: Commentators place the film in a tradition of romances between humans and monsters, where desire and difference can unsettle social expectations. The i Paper review calls the story sexist in its depiction of the husband’s lack of agency, but says Colman’s character’s relief at having a kind, supportive partner gives the fantasy its appeal.

perspectives.body: The i Paper reviewer finds Wicker’s husband troublingly without agency, yet enjoys the film’s bawdy comedy and its fantasy of a man who supports his wife without expecting subordination in return.

content.headline: Alex Cox on independent film, Bond and the chaos of Sid and Nancy
content.shortHeadline: Alex Cox on Sid and Nancy, Bond and indie filmmaking
content.standfirst: The director revisits his cult films, explains why he is crowdfunding Repo Man 2 and offers blunt views on franchises. He also recalls John Lydon’s furious response to Sid and Nancy.

image.caption: Alex Cox.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Cox: ‘John Lydon said Sid and Nancy was a nightmarish piece of garbage’

segments.body: In a question-and-answer interview, Alex Cox recalls that John Lydon called the Sid and Nancy script a “nightmarish piece of garbage”. Cox says Lydon also advised him to fictionalise the story further, and that the resulting controversy proved useful when the film came out.

segments.title: Keeping films independent
segments.body: Cox is crowdfunding Repo Man 2, set in a world of driverless cars. He argues that independent filmmakers have reason to seek support directly from audiences, saying studios and large streamers are more interested in franchises and intellectual property than in scripts. He also gives an unsparing assessment of contemporary franchise filmmaking.

content.headline: Guarding Stars makes holiday-romance silliness work
content.shortHeadline: Leighton Meester shines in Guarding Stars
content.standfirst: Leighton Meester brings wit and warmth to a familiar Christmas romcom formula about a bodyguard and a movie star. The review finds the film’s silliness part of its appeal.

image.caption: Leighton Meester and Jared Padalecki in Guarding Stars.

sources.originalTitle: Guarding Stars review – Leighton Meester is a delight in fizzy Netflix holiday romance

segments.body: Leighton Meester plays a no-nonsense bodyguard assigned to protect a film star at his family’s Montana ranch. The setup is far-fetched, the review concedes, but Meester’s sharp performance gives Hannah enough personality to make the predictable holiday-romance beats enjoyable.

The film follows familiar seasonal conventions—an awkward fake relationship, a family gathering and a late romantic turn—but adds brisk action and a warm supporting cast. The review says Meester’s performance makes the combination of female competence and Christmas sentiment work better than expected.

content.headline: The Altruists makes a chaotic crypto scandal compelling television
content.shortHeadline: The Altruists turns the FTX scandal into tense TV
content.standfirst: Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle play Caroline Ellison and Sam Bankman-Fried in a fast-moving account of FTX’s rise and collapse. The review praises the performances while warning that the financial detail can be hard to follow.

image.caption: Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists.

sources.originalTitle: The Altruists review – two of TV’s best actors light up this chaotic crypto tale

segments.body: The Altruists traces the relationship between Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison from their early work together to FTX’s collapse. The series links their commitment to effective altruism with the self-image and rationalisations that surround their decisions, as the company’s apparent idealism gives way to fraud and financial ruin.

segments.title: A high-wire performance
segments.body: The Guardian review praises Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner, and says their performances keep the series just coherent enough to follow. It finds some of the financial mechanics difficult to grasp, but sees the show’s larger subject as the danger of concentrating wealth and power in people who believe they are acting for the greater good.

content.headline: I Am Helen puts the women harmed by toxic masculinity in focus
content.shortHeadline: I Am Helen centres women’s experience of toxic masculinity
content.standfirst: Nicola Coughlan plays a woman whose partner’s misogynistic ideas turn into coercion and violence. The review argues that the drama’s unsettling force lies in showing how ordinary the behaviour can appear.

image.caption: Nicola Coughlan as Helen and Joe Cole as Steve in I Am Helen.

sources.originalTitle: All men should watch I Am Helen

segments.body: The latest instalment of Dominic Savage’s anthology follows Helen, played by Nicola Coughlan, as her partner Steve’s seemingly ordinary grievances harden into controlling behaviour. A non-consensual act of violence is followed by him casting himself as the victim, and Helen is left apologising as their life appears to return to normal.

segments.title: The ordinary roots of harm
segments.body: The review argues that the drama’s most disturbing scenes show misogyny seeping into daily life: a colleague’s advice and familiar claims of male victimhood help Steve justify his expectations of women. It says the story shifts attention from destructive men to the women who bear the consequences.

content.headline: The Last Spy finds a complicated history behind a CIA career
content.shortHeadline: The Last Spy follows Peter Sichel through cold war history
content.standfirst: A long interview with refugee-turned-CIA officer Peter Sichel gives this documentary an extraordinary central voice. The review also notes what remains unknowable about his work and the people he recruited.

image.caption: Peter Sichel in The Last Spy.

sources.originalTitle: The Last Spy review – a riveting tale of CIA meddling, espionage gossip and Blue Nun wine

segments.body: Peter Sichel recounts fleeing Germany with his family, joining the US army and becoming a German-speaking intelligence officer. The documentary follows his career through the emergence of the CIA and the cold war, while Sichel’s dry, candid account keeps the history rooted in one life.

segments.title: The secrets left untold
segments.body: The Guardian review finds Sichel’s changing views on communism and US power more revealing than a conventional spy adventure. But he keeps quiet about what he and his agents did, leaving the documentary with an unresolved gap between the historical importance of his work and the details he will disclose.

content.headline: Heated Rivalry’s 4DX screenings turn romance into a physical gag
content.shortHeadline: Heated Rivalry fans test its 4DX thrills
content.standfirst: Fans in hockey jerseys watched episodes of the romance in seats that moved, vibrated and sprayed water. The experience was often ridiculous and funny, though one viewer said the effects could undercut the emotion.

image.caption: Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams in Heated Rivalry.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I hope paramedics are on standby for the sex scenes!’ The wet and wild TV experience leaving fans dizzy

segments.body: Cineworld’s 4DX screenings of Heated Rivalry paired episodes of the queer hockey romance with moving seats, water, wind and other sensory effects. Fans interviewed at the event arrived curious about how the technology would handle the show’s hockey scenes, text messages and intimate moments.

segments.title: A very silly spectacle
segments.body: The crowd laughed as seat vibrations accompanied messages and the audience was splashed during a scene by a lake. Some movement worked better than others, and one fan said the effects could distract from the emotional story. For many in the room, though, the absurdity was precisely the appeal.

content.headline: December’s TV highlights include new Austen and Harry Potter adaptations
content.shortHeadline: What to watch on TV this December
content.standfirst: A BBC guide to the month’s new series ranges from Pride and Prejudice and Harry Potter to returning comedies and crime dramas, with international streaming dates included.

sources.originalTitle: Harry Potter to Pride and Prejudice: 10 of the best TV shows to watch this December

segments.body: The December selection includes new adaptations of Pride and Prejudice and Harry Potter, alongside a return for Only Murders in the Building and a holiday special for The Other Bennet Sister. The guide gives cast details and describes how each production approaches familiar stories and characters.

segments.title: More to stream
segments.body: The list also covers a submarine thriller, a JonBenét Ramsey drama, a story of the Indian diaspora in the US, and returning shows including Emily in Paris. Each entry includes premiere information for the services and regions supplied in the guide.

content.headline: Why Grand Theft Auto is unlikely to become a TV series
content.shortHeadline: Why Grand Theft Auto may never work as a TV series
content.standfirst: Take-Two says an adaptation would need to delight players, but this essay argues that GTA’s open-ended play is the very thing a scripted series would struggle to preserve.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto would be a huge TV series – here’s why it will never happen

segments.body: Take-Two chief executive Strauss Zelnick says a film or television adaptation of Grand Theft Auto is not ruled out, but would need to engage and delight players. The Guardian essay argues that the game’s appeal comes from the freedom for different players to have radically different experiences—something a single scripted narrative would flatten.

segments.title: Some worlds resist adaptation
segments.body: The piece compares GTA with works such as Maus and Calvin and Hobbes, whose creators have argued that their original forms serve them best. It also notes that those refusals may not last forever, pointing to One Hundred Years of Solitude, which reached television after its author had died.

content.headline: GTA VI tips for players—and why its 18 rating matters
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI: practical tips and a warning for parents
content.standfirst: A guide to avoiding trouble in Leonida offers advice on cash, heat and heists, while a separate report details the game’s explicit sex, drugs and violence. Both make clear that the sprawling new world is made for adults.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto VI, an adults-only game.

sources.originalTitle: Bank your stolen cash, bring a change of clothes, go easy on the bloodshed: 15 tips for playing Grand Theft Auto VI
‘Definitely one of the best games I’ve ever played’: our games editor answered your GTA VI questions
Parents: please don’t buy Grand Theft Auto VI for your child

segments.title: Getting around Leonida
segments.body: The Guardian’s guide recommends banking cash at ATMs, using a getaway car rather than your own for crimes, and changing clothes or vehicles to reduce police attention. It also advises players to use checkpoint retries during missions, avoid unnecessary violence and take their time with the large game.

segments.title: An adults-only world
segments.body: A separate report warns parents that GTA VI’s 18 rating reflects far more than violence: it describes explicit sex, full-frontal nudity, drugs and vulgar dialogue. The games editor similarly tells parents to consider the material and their teenager’s exposure before deciding whether the game is appropriate.

content.headline: The Wii and PlayStation 3 imagined gaming’s future in different ways
content.shortHeadline: The Wii and PS3 offered rival visions of gaming
content.standfirst: Twenty years on, the Wii’s accessible motion controls and the PS3’s technical ambition both look influential—and incomplete. This retrospective traces what each console got right and where its vision fell short.

image.caption: Nintendo’s Wii and Sony’s PlayStation 3.

sources.originalTitle: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?

segments.body: Nintendo’s Wii made motion controls and accessible play its pitch, with Wii Sports turning the console into a fixture of family gatherings. Sony’s PlayStation 3 promised technical power, online connectivity and long, ambitious games, while also supporting independent developers.

segments.title: Two legacies
segments.body: The retrospective argues that neither company’s vision fully won: gaming now includes both intuitive, accessible experiences and enormous, demanding adventures. The Wii sold more consoles, while the PS3 helped set foundations for online play and technically ambitious games; each also left parts of its promise unrealised.

content.headline: Can an Elden Ring film make its bleak fantasy world matter?
content.shortHeadline: The challenge facing an Elden Ring film
content.standfirst: Alex Garland’s adaptation has a major game, a prominent mythology and a reported large budget behind it. The challenge, this essay argues, is making audiences care about the world rather than merely explaining it.

image.caption: Elden Ring, the game being adapted for film.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation is on course to be Hollywood’s goriest ever fantasy movie

segments.body: The forthcoming Elden Ring adaptation is written and directed by Alex Garland and has a cast that includes Cailee Spaeny, Ben Whishaw, Nick Offerman and Jonathan Pryce. The game has sold more than 30 million copies, but its vast world and grim, often horrific imagery make the move to film a difficult one.

segments.title: World-building is not enough
segments.body: The essay compares the project with fantasy adaptations that struggled to turn elaborate source material into compelling cinema. Garland’s films have resisted conventional reassurance, but the piece raises the question of whether that approach can survive the reported scale of this production—and what kind of story could give viewers a reason to stay in the Lands Between.

content.headline: Colibactin toxin emerges as a leading suspect in early-onset bowel cancer
content.shortHeadline: A gut toxin is a leading suspect in bowel cancer under 50
content.standfirst: Researchers told MPs that early exposure to colibactin, produced by some E coli, may help explain rising bowel cancer rates in younger people. Its role remains under investigation.

image.caption: E coli bacteria in the gut; some variants produce the toxin colibactin, a suspected contributor to early-onset bowel cancer.

sources.originalTitle: Bacterial toxin produced by E coli leading suspect in rise in bowel cancer among under-50s

segments.body: Bowel cancer cases among people under 50 have doubled in many countries over the past two decades. Known risks such as obesity, smoking and alcohol explain only about half of cases, researchers told a parliamentary committee, prompting a search for other causes.

segments.title: A clue, not a conclusion
segments.body: Colibactin, a toxin made by some E coli in the gut, is a leading suspect. Mutations associated with the toxin were three times more common in tumours from people under 40 than in those over 70. Scientists are investigating whether it drives cancer; they have not established that it does. Evidence of mutations in some children raises the possibility that exposure early in life could matter.

Researchers also said that established risks remain important. Cancer epidemiologist Elio Riboli told MPs that applying what is already known about prevention could avert many cancers, even as scientists work to identify other causes.

content.headline: Dispute over IPCC report timing puts climate science and global stocktake at a ‘
content.shortHeadline: IPCC report delay risks disrupting climate negotiations
content.standfirst: Some countries want to delay the next major climate assessment until after a 2028 review of Paris pledges. Scientists and negotiators warn that slowing the work could complicate cooperation and weaken the process.

sources.originalTitle: IPCC report delay will threaten global effort to tackle climate crisis, says top scientist

segments.body: The next comprehensive assessment by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change is under way, with completion hoped for in 2028. Its findings are expected to inform that year’s global stocktake of progress under the Paris agreement, which will assess whether countries’ emissions pledges are sufficient.

segments.title: A contested timetable
segments.body: Russia, India and the Arab group, including Saudi Arabia, have argued for publication in 2029, after the stocktake. They say developing countries are disadvantaged in the process, and some critics describe the IPCC’s mitigation scenarios as biased against the global south. Climate scientist Johan Rockström rejects that charge and says the pathways reflect peer-reviewed evidence.

The IPCC says 51% of the 664 appointed report authors come from developing countries and economies in transition. Some developing countries, including small island states and least developed countries, want the report completed without delay. The IPCC’s budget is also under discussion; without an agreement, producing the assessment in time for the stocktake could become harder.

content.headline: Small keto study for anorexia prompts questions about evidence and private money
content.shortHeadline: Anorexia keto study raises questions about evidence and funding
content.standfirst: A small trial found symptom improvements for some participants, but it cannot establish that a restrictive diet treats anorexia. The investigation also examines how a wealthy family’s funding may shape the research agenda.

sources.originalTitle: Roblox money is pushing a controversial anorexia treatment

segments.body: A 14-week study explored whether a ketogenic diet was safe and feasible for people with anorexia; it was not designed to prove the diet works. Of 22 people recruited, 18 completed the trial. Twelve no longer met the study’s diagnostic criteria for anorexia at the end, and the lead researcher said none lost weight. The trial did not compare the diet with standard treatment.

segments.title: Caution about a restrictive diet
segments.body: Psychiatrists and nutrition experts interviewed by The Verge warned that the findings are too limited to support claims of effectiveness. They note that restricting food may be risky for people with eating disorders, and that some participants’ symptoms worsened. Researchers say larger, controlled trials are needed; experts also stress that the study does not justify replacing established care.

segments.title: Who sets the research agenda?
segments.body: The report traces substantial private funding from the Baszucki family for ketogenic-diet research and raises questions about how philanthropic priorities can steer a field, especially as public research funding falls. The family’s spokesperson said its focus is on interventions that government and industry have been slow to support; the reporting also details disagreements about how the evidence and one patient’s treatment story were presented.

content.headline: NHS hospitals prepare to offer Alzheimer’s blood tests before trials report
content.shortHeadline: Some NHS hospitals plan Alzheimer’s blood tests before trial results
content.standfirst: Blood tests may speed up assessment for people with memory problems, but access is likely to vary. Two large trials are still under way, and the tests should be used as part of clinical assessment rather than as a stand-alone diagnosis.

sources.originalTitle: The simple test that will diagnose Alzheimer’s within days – available next year

segments.body: Some UK hospitals plan to introduce blood tests for Alzheimer’s in memory clinics and neurology departments, potentially shortening a diagnosis that can take months or years. University College Hospital in London is already offering the test, and Manchester Brain Health Centre says it expects to start within weeks.

segments.title: Access and limits
segments.body: The test measures a form of tau protein, which can help clinicians assess whether Alzheimer’s is likely and distinguish it from some other causes of memory problems. Two large trials examining how the tests fit into NHS services are due to finish in 2029. There is no central list of hospitals offering the service, raising the possibility of uneven access.

Doctors say results need to be interpreted alongside clinical and cognitive assessments. Private testing outside a memory clinic could produce false positives, while a blood test may help rule out Alzheimer’s when symptoms have another cause. Faster identification could support care planning and help some people access trials or treatment options.

content.headline: Wreck of Australia’s first locally built warship found 128 years after sinking
content.shortHeadline: Australia’s first locally built warship found after 128 years
content.standfirst: Marine archaeologists found the wooden gunboat Spitfire off Queensland on the anniversary of its 1898 sinking. The wreck is protected, adding a newly located vessel to Australia’s maritime heritage.

image.caption: Illustration of the HMCS Spitfire, Australia’s first locally built warship.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Remarkable luck’: wreck of first Australian-built warship discovered exactly 128 years after sinking

segments.body: The wreck of the 19-metre Spitfire was found off far north Queensland on 21 August, exactly 128 years after it sank. A team from the Australian National Maritime Museum, Queensland government and Royal Australian Navy located it using sonar during a month-long search guided by archival records.

segments.title: A vessel with changing roles
segments.body: Built in Sydney in 1855, the gunboat was commissioned by the colonial government amid concern about Russian and French military presence in the region. It later served Queensland as a pilot vessel before being sold for use in sea-cucumber fishing. The crew were rescued when it foundered in 1898.

content.headline: UK tribunal orders government to confirm secret Apple encryption order
content.shortHeadline: UK government ordered to confirm secret Apple data order
content.standfirst: A tribunal has rejected the Home Office’s claim that confirming the order would harm national security. The government has yet to confirm it, and a further hearing is expected to consider what details can be made public.

sources.originalTitle: UK government forced to disclose secret Apple backdoor order

segments.body: The UK Investigatory Powers Tribunal has ordered the government to confirm that it issued Apple a secret order seeking access to encrypted customer data. The tribunal rejected the Home Office’s argument that disclosure of the order’s existence would damage national security. The Home Office has not yet confirmed the notice.

segments.title: A dispute over encryption and disclosure
segments.body: Apple challenged the order and blocked UK users from enabling its Advanced Data Protection feature for iCloud rather than comply. The reported demand was later narrowed to British nationals’ data stored in Apple’s encrypted cloud. Apple has said it has never built a backdoor or master key and never will; it did not comment after the ruling.

The case was brought by Liberty International on behalf of two individuals. The group says this is the first known time the government has been compelled to confirm the existence of a secret technical order. A final hearing on which details can be released is expected next year.

content.headline: US senators press Apple, Google and Meta over access to AI ‘nudify’ apps
content.shortHeadline: Senators challenge tech firms over AI ‘nudify’ apps
content.standfirst: Three senators say apps and ads that can generate non-consensual sexual images remain accessible to children despite company rules. The firms say they prohibit the content and are working to detect it.

image.caption: Senators Ed Markey and Ron Wyden at a news conference at the Capitol.

sources.originalTitle: Senators criticize Apple and Google for letting teens access ‘nudify’ apps despite parental controls

segments.body: US senators Ron Wyden, Ed Markey and Ben Luján have asked Apple, Google and Meta to explain how apps and advertisements promoting AI-generated nude imagery continue to reach users, including children. Their letters cite research by the Tech Transparency Project, which found apps on the two companies’ stores and ads on Meta platforms.

segments.title: Rules and enforcement under scrutiny
segments.body: Researchers said they accessed 135 apps through accounts they presented as belonging to 13-year-old boys. Apple and Google removed apps named in the research after being contacted, but the apps remained functional on phones where they had already been installed. Meta says it prohibits promotion of nudification apps and has removed large numbers of sexual ads; the senators question whether its review systems are catching violations.

Google says it continually works to detect and remove harmful apps. Apple has said developers may add prohibited features after an app is approved. The senators argue that clarifying policies is not enough if the apps and ads keep appearing, and say Congress may need to act if companies do not improve enforcement.

content.headline: UK actors’ union wins consent and pay protections for digital replicas
content.shortHeadline: UK actors gain consent and pay rights over digital replicas
content.standfirst: A new agreement with film and television producers would require project-specific consent and payment when performers’ digital replicas are used. It does not establish explicit protections for using performances to train AI systems.

sources.originalTitle: Actors in UK to get more rights over their ‘digital replicas’ in deal on AI protections

segments.body: A deal between actors’ union Equity and Producers Alliance for Cinema and Television gives performers the right to consent to, and be paid for, use of their digital replicas. Contracts will specify permission for an individual project rather than blanket consent. The agreement also sets rules for substantial digital changes to scenes involving agreed levels of nudity or simulated sexual activity.

segments.title: What the agreement leaves open
segments.body: The three-year deal will go to a vote of 8,000 Equity members, with the union’s leadership recommending approval. It does not create explicit contractual protections for using actors’ performances to train AI systems. Equity also says it cannot cover some digital scanning traditionally done for visual effects added later in production.

content.headline: JPMorgan says vendor cyberattack exposed some customer marketing data
content.shortHeadline: JPMorgan says vendor breach may have exposed customer names
content.standfirst: The bank says attackers accessed marketing data held by third-party vendors, potentially including names and email addresses. It says the breach was unrelated to a recent service outage and has not found evidence that payment data was affected.

sources.originalTitle: JPMorgan Chase reveals data breach, but says it’s unrelated to this week’s banking outage

segments.body: JPMorgan Chase says third-party vendors providing services to the bank were targeted in a cyberattack. Its investigation indicates attackers accessed some marketing data, which may include customer names and email addresses. The bank says it will contact affected customers where appropriate and offer support, including credit monitoring.

segments.title: Other firms report vendor incidents
segments.body: Cybernews reported that a dataset may include information on about 16,000 JPMorgan customers, though the figure has not been independently confirmed in the supplied reporting. Visa and Mastercard also confirmed attacks affecting a third-party vendor. Visa said there was no indication payment-card data was affected; Mastercard described a limited amount of information from some cardholders in a specific benefits programme.
JPMorgan says the breach has no connection to a recent outage, which it attributed to a software bug. It also says its services were not disrupted by the cyberattack.

content.headline: Anthropic’s $81bn IPO tests its finances, safety promises and governance
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic’s record IPO tests its safety promises and business model
content.standfirst: The Claude maker’s public debut raises unprecedented sums, but its huge compute commitments, supplier-investors and unusual oversight structure leave questions about whether its safety mission can withstand pressure to grow.

sources.originalTitle: Anthropic to begin public trading at $1.5tn valuation after largest-ever IPO
Anthropic’s IPO puts AI’s circular financing boom to the test
With the biggest IPO of all time, Anthropic’s ‘good guy’ reputation is on the line
At Nasdaq opening bell, Anthropic CEO recommits to pacing AI development

segments.body: Anthropic began public trading after raising $81.3bn in an upsized share sale priced at $83, giving it a fully diluted market value of about $1.5tn. The first frontier AI lab to go public, it is now a test of investor appetite for the technology as well as the company’s ability to turn rapid growth into lasting returns. Its filing reported $104bn in losses for the first nine months of 2026.

segments.title: Investors and suppliers intertwined
segments.body: Amazon and Google are both major investors in Anthropic and providers of infrastructure it uses. Other technology companies also committed $26bn in a private placement. Critics describe this overlap as circular financing: money invested in the AI company can flow back to suppliers when it pays for computing. Analysts cited by TechCrunch say the public listing and other customers could make the model more sustainable, but Anthropic has committed to $900bn in spending, primarily on compute and infrastructure.

perspectives.body: Analysts differ on the risk: one described the arrangements as still adding value to the ecosystem, while another argued that suppliers such as Amazon and Google could benefit even if Anthropic loses its lead.

segments.title: Who can hold the company to its mission?
segments.body: Anthropic’s public-benefit status and Long-Term Benefit Trust are intended to balance public benefit against shareholder returns. But The Verge’s examination of its filings and interviews with experts questions how much power the trust has to intervene, and whether its trustees have the expertise to assess AI development.
